how: Pre-register before looking at data: test-data/claim-tests/README.md. Log results with delphi_log_test_result or a pull request.

claims.title: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claims.statement: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.

claims.title: Habituation (pharmacoresistance) occurs in every testable pathway model
claims.statement: Modelling pharmacoresistance as habituation (a progressive 50% drop in response across repeated, lengthening stimulations), at least one habituating stimulus–response pair was found in each of the 27 testable BioModels pathway models, with 1–50% of node pairs per model habituating.

claims.title: Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall
claims.statement: In the surveyed ODE pathway models with UCS-based memory, most networks retain the bulk of their memories over waiting periods up to 100 times the initial one, and testing (recalling) a memory generally does not destroy it and in rare cases strengthens it.

claims.title: Published ODE models of gene and protein pathways show several kinds of memory
claims.statement: In simulations of 35 published ODE models of gene regulatory networks and protein/metabolic pathways from BioModels, the networks show several distinct kinds of memory (UCS-based, pairing, transfer, associative and consolidation memory) in response to patterns of node stimulation.

claims.title: Stimulating other nodes can break pharmacoresistance in many pathway models
claims.statement: In 17 of the 27 habituating BioModels pathway models (about 63%), stimulating a third node (neither the stimulus nor the response) abolished habituation for some stimulus–response pairs, so some biological networks contain discoverable stimulus nodes that may serve to break pharmacoresistance without rewiring the network.

claims.title: Pathway memories can form through dynamics alone, without structural change
claims.statement: In ODE models of biological pathways, memories (such as associative memory, in which a neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus) can be formed by patterns of stimulation through dynamical interactions alone, without changing the network's structure or parameters.

claims.title: Serially trained associative memories cause catastrophic forgetting in pathway models
claims.statement: When two associative memories are trained one after another in ODE pathway models, all biological and random models show catastrophic forgetting in which both memories are lost, whereas two UCS-based memories can be stored serially or in parallel.

claims.title: Sensitization is harder to break than habituation in pathway models
claims.statement: In ODE pathway models, sensitization could be broken by stimulating a third node in only 8 of 27 sensitizing models, mostly for fewer than 5% of node pairs, so breaking sensitization is less likely than breaking habituation and therapies may need other avenues of intervention.

claims.title: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claims.statement: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.

claims.title: Pathway-model memories are robust to a wide range of stimulus strengths
claims.statement: In the surveyed ODE pathway models, memory formation is robust to training stimuli of 10x, 50x and 100x baseline (most models kept the same number of memories and only 10% lost memories), and some models formed more memories with weaker stimulation.

claims.title: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
claims.statement: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.

claims.title: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claims.statement: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.

claims.title: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
claims.statement: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.

claims.title: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
claims.statement: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

claims.title: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
claims.statement: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.

claims.title: Evolution changes the competency gene more often than any structural gene
claims.statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model with evolvable competency, positional changes to cells over 1000 generations resulted from changes to the competency gene significantly more often than from changes to any of the fifty structural genes.

claims.title: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
claims.statement: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.

claims.title: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.

claims.title: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
claims.statement: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.

claims.title: No simple network-topology measure predicts memory in pathway models
claims.statement: Across the 35 surveyed BioModels pathway models, the amount of memory showed no significant correlation with mean number of nodes, edges, degree or hubness, so no single network property is indicative of memory.

claims.title: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claims.statement: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.

claims.title: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
claims.statement: The fundamental agreement in structure among organisms of the same class, independent of their habits of life, is explained by their common descent.

claims.title: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
claims.statement: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.

claims.title: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claims.statement: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.

claims.title: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
claims.statement: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.
